claims.text: Pre-coating tungsten particles with nickel before copper infiltration will improve interfacial wetting.
The nickel coating will improve interfacial bonding during transient liquid-phase sintering.
Nickel pre-coating will reduce phase separation and void formation in W–Cu composites.
A uniform nickel coating 50–100 nm thick is an appropriate intervention for tungsten particles.
Processing at approximately 1100–1200 °C is sufficient to melt copper while remaining well below tungsten's melting point.
Fusion-reactor joint service can be represented by moderate thermal loads below 700 °C together with irradiation exposure.
The nickel coating promotes formation of a thin interfacial intermetallic layer between tungsten and copper.
The proposed interfacial layer lowers interfacial tension.
Lower interfacial tension enhances infiltration of liquid copper into the tungsten structure.
Enhanced infiltration minimizes void formation and suppresses phase segregation.
Nickel acts as an active wetting agent for molten copper on refractory tungsten.
Nickel reduces the surface-energy difference between molten copper and tungsten.
More uniform wetting leads to improved interfacial bonding and reduced porosity.
Improved bonding and reduced porosity enhance thermal transport.
Improved bonding and reduced porosity enhance mechanical durability under irradiation.
Relative to untreated spark-plasma-sintered or additively manufactured W–Cu, the Ni-coated composite will have a denser microstructure and lower void volume fraction.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the Ni-coated composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the Ni-coated composite will show improved mechanical durability under simulated fusion-relevant irradiation.
Conventional spark-plasma-sintered or metal-3D-printed W–Cu without interfacial treatment typically suffers from poor wetting, phase separation, and void formation.
